title: AI-First Workflows for Clinical Study Reporting
text:
Welcome
Welcome to a practical guide to AI-first workflows for clinical study reports.
This book explores how organizations can move from isolated AI adoption toward an AI-native way of working by building AI-first workflows across clinical study reports. In these workflows, an AI agent performs a bounded, repeatable first pass; people define and monitor the process, review the evidence, and remain responsible for decisions.
The focus is not a particular model or software stack. Instead, it is on durable principles that teams can adapt to their own technology, governance, and operating environment.
The book is written for people who design, perform, review, or govern clinical study reports and want to integrate AI systematically into their work. No prior experience building AI agents is required. Familiarity with clinical study artifacts and review processes will help readers connect the examples to their own work.

title: AI-First Workflows for Clinical Study Reporting
text:
How to use this book
The main route is reading: begin with the Introduction (Chapters 1–4), then follow the applied examples in order. Each example states its teaching purpose, maturity, and prerequisites up front.

Main route (no setup required). Read the chapters in order and work the exercises through a browser-based AI agent. You will specify requirements and review prepared code and results; no local R, Python, Git, or Codespaces setup is required on this route.
Technical route (optional). If you want to run the materials yourself, the day-one exercise and the rounding prototype described in Chapters 5–7 give you synthetic data, scripts, and expected results. Contributor setup is documented in the repository README.
Facilitator route. Shared worksheets, completed examples, and assessment rubrics are linked from the exercise chapters as they become available.

title: 1  AI-first workflows in Biometrics
text:
1.1 From AI adoption to AI-first
Clinical trial development is already organized as a chain of connected workflows. The study protocol informs trial operations and the statistical analysis plan (SAP). Collected data move through the Study Data Tabulation Model (SDTM) and Analysis Data Model (ADaM) into tables, listings, and figures (TLFs). Those results support the clinical study report and regulatory submission. Every step has inputs, rules, handoffs, reviews, and accountable owners.
AI can do more than accelerate one isolated task. An agent can inspect artifacts, use tools, execute several steps, observe results, and return evidence-backed findings or recommendations. Using that capability reliably requires the surrounding workflow to be designed for human-agent collaboration.
In this book, an AI-first workflow is a bounded, repeatable process designed for an AI agent to perform structured work with tools, while explicit artifacts, rules, events, benchmarks, and human decision rights govern its execution and improvement.
AI adoption begins when an individual uses AI for an isolated task inside an existing workflow. A person decides when to invoke AI, assembles the context, reviews the response, and moves the work forward. This can improve personal productivity, but the workflow itself remains unchanged. The KEYNOTE-189 demonstration in Chapter 3 uses this pattern to show what a single prompt can accomplish and why a repeatable workflow needs more than a prompt.
An AI-first workflow begins with the work rather than the model. The team defines the objective, boundary, evidence, success measures, and decision rights, then assigns each step to the component best suited to perform it. AI does not need to perform every task or make final decisions.

title: 1  AI-first workflows in Biometrics
text:
1.2 How an AI-first workflow works
An AI-first workflow does not begin and end with a prompt. It connects AI to a repeatable process:

Event -> Task -> Tools and agent -> Evidence -> Human decision -> Recorded state

An event starts the workflow, such as a change to an SAP, dataset, program, or output. The task definition states the objective, source artifacts, allowed tools, expected result, conditions for stopping, and responsible reviewer.
The workflow gives the agent current, versioned artifacts instead of relying on whatever happens to be available in a chat. The agent returns a structured finding that states what was checked, the supporting evidence, any uncertainty, and what it could not cover. A human reviews the finding, makes the decision, and records that decision for the next run.
The design separates three kinds of work:







Work
Best-suited component




Apply an exact rule, calculation, or comparison
Deterministic software


Interpret written requirements, trace context, or plan variable steps
AI agent


Exercise domain judgment, approve policy, or accept accountability
Human role



The simplest capable component should perform each step. An AI agent should not replace a deterministic test, and access to a tool should never be confused with approval authority. Chapter 2 develops the design principles that make this division of work inspectable and trustworthy.

title: 1  AI-first workflows in Biometrics
text:
1.3 Human accountability is not optional
In an AI-first workflow, the human role shifts from manually executing every step toward defining the work, supervising agents and tools, reviewing exceptions, challenging evidence, and improving the workflow. The agent can retrieve, compare, draft, run approved tools, and monitor routine conditions. The accountable human retains responsibility for the decision and its consequences.
This makes three human capabilities especially valuable: systems thinking, end-to-end knowledge, and exception handling.






WarningAI output is not regulatory clearance



An April 2026 FDA warning letter to Purolea Cosmetics Lab described a drug manufacturer that used AI agents to create specifications, procedures, and production records. FDA found that the firm had not adequately reviewed the generated documents for accuracy and Current Good Manufacturing Practice (CGMP) compliance. The firm also reportedly relied on the agent’s failure to mention a requirement as a reason for not knowing that the requirement applied.
The letter concerns pharmaceutical manufacturing and CGMP, not clinical study reporting. Its workflow lesson still transfers: AI-generated content remains a draft until an authorized person verifies and approves it. The workflow must check authoritative requirements, disclose what it did not cover, and preserve the evidence behind the decision. An agent cannot be the source of regulatory truth or its own approver.

title: 1  AI-first workflows in Biometrics

1.4 Where AI-first workflows apply in Biometrics
AI-first workflows can support each Biometrics pillar without changing who is accountable for the work.








Pillar
Useful first pass

Data management

Many valuable workflows cross these boundaries. Reviewing a TLF may require the SAP, ADaM metadata, executed code, rendered output, and prior decisions. Domain expertise and end-to-end knowledge therefore become more important, not less.

title: 1  AI-first workflows in Biometrics
text:
1.5 Start with one bounded workflow
An organization does not need to begin with autonomous, end-to-end execution. A useful first workflow is small enough to observe closely but valuable enough to improve real work. It has a clear beginning and end, accessible source artifacts, a reviewable output, and a named person responsible for the decision.
A workflow is bounded when the team can state:

what event starts it;
which artifacts and tools it may use;
which actions the agent may take;
what output it must return;
when it must stop or escalate; and
who reviews the result and makes the decision.

The initial implementation should include a task contract, a deterministic foundation wherever exact rules can be encoded, and a reviewable result. It can begin in advisory mode and expand one boundary at a time. The applied examples develop these implementations through the shared AI-first SDLC rather than introducing a separate development sequence for each workflow.
For example, a first workflow for reviewing a changed table could be defined as follows:







Element
Definition




Trigger
A pull request changes a table program or rendered output


Inputs
Current SAP, output specification, analysis metadata, source code, and rendered table


Agent task
Compare the change with the requirements and identify inconsistencies or missing evidence


Required output
Structured findings with source references, coverage, uncertainty, and recommended follow-up


Stop conditions
A required artifact is missing, versions conflict, or the finding requires statistical judgment


Human decision
The accountable reviewer accepts, rejects, or investigates each finding



This workflow is deliberately narrow, but it establishes reusable capabilities: artifact retrieval, traceable review, structured findings, escalation, and a recorded human decision. Those capabilities become the foundation for broader AI-first workflows and for the lifecycle described in Chapter 4.

title: 2  Principles of trustworthy assistance
text:
2.1 Root principle: Trustworthy assistance
Chapter 1 defines an AI-first workflow as a bounded process in which artifacts, rules, events, benchmarks, and human decision rights govern an agent’s work. This chapter develops the principles that make such a workflow inspectable, repeatable, and reviewable.
Agents are bounded human assistants. Their exact role depends on the example: an agent may draft, calculate, compare, review, or monitor within its assigned boundary. In a code-review workflow, for example, an agent may act as an independent reviewer assistant. It does not make final statistical decisions, approve deliverables, or replace the responsible human role.
The root principle of an AI-first workflow is trustworthy assistance.
Trustworthy assistance means the agent’s work can be inspected, repeated, challenged, and reviewed. The agent should not rely on hidden memory, unsupported claims, or vague reasoning. It should work from visible artifacts, preserve explicit state, act through defined events and rules, use tools to gather evidence, and escalate judgment to accountable humans.
The five principles below translate trustworthy assistance into a practical design pattern.

title: 2  Principles of trustworthy assistance
text: A workflow is trustworthy when its inputs are visible, its actions are traceable, its findings are evidence-backed, and its limits are clear.

title: 2  Principles of trustworthy assistance
text:
2.2 Principle 1: Inspectable artifacts
Trust requires the agent and humans to inspect the same source materials.
Artifacts should be readable, structured where possible, versioned, citable, and diffable. Examples include:

SAP sections that are searchable and citable;
ADaM metadata that expose dataset names, variable names, labels, types, codelists, and analysis flags;
TLF outputs with stable table identifiers, titles, footnotes, and source references; and
findings stored as structured records rather than only narrative comments.


If the agent cannot inspect the work, it cannot reliably assist with the work.

title: 2  Principles of trustworthy assistance
2  Principles of trustworthy assistance
text:
2.4 Principle 3: Events and rules
Trust requires predictable triggers rather than random or purely chat-driven action. An event indicates that something changed. A rule determines what the workflow should do next.



Event
Rule




SAP section updated
Rerun affected SAP-to-TLF checks


ADaM metadata changed
Rerun checks that use the changed variables


ADaM dataset refreshed
Rerun affected population and value checks


TLF output regenerated
Rerun affected TLF checks


Human requests a recheck
Run the requested review


Another agent changes a deliverable
Verify downstream impact



Without explicit triggers, review coverage depends on someone remembering to ask. Events and rules make the workflow easier to repeat and explain.

Events trigger attention; rules trigger action.

title: 2  Principles of trustworthy assistance
2  Principles of trustworthy assistance
text:
2.6 Principle 5: Human judgment
Trust requires clear accountability. AI-first does not mean AI-only.
An agent may identify discrepancies, assemble evidence, classify likely severity, and recommend follow-up. The accountable human decides whether a finding is valid, whether an artifact should change, and how the decision should be recorded.
The agent should stop or escalate when language is ambiguous, a required artifact is missing, evidence conflicts, a decision requires domain judgment, or the workflow rule does not cover the case.

Agents prepare evidence; humans make accountable decisions.

title: 2  Principles of trustworthy assistance
section: 2.7 Preview: Change review across SAP, code, and results
text:
2.7 Preview: Change review across SAP, code, and results
A future applied example will use change management across the SAP, analysis code, and results to show how the principles work together. This is a useful preview because a change in one artifact can affect several downstream decisions.







Principle
Requirement for the future example




Inspectable artifacts
Provide versioned SAP requirements, code, metadata, and rendered results


Explicit state
Record changed artifacts and classify findings as new, fixed, acknowledged, or unresolved


Events and rules
Trigger only the checks affected by an accepted change


Tools and evidence
Compare expected and observed behavior and cite the supporting artifacts


Human judgment
Escalate ambiguity and preserve the accountable reviewer’s decision



The full example will define the workflow boundary, inputs, expected outputs, benchmarks, stopping conditions, and lifecycle artifacts. Keeping those details with the example avoids turning this principles chapter into a second workflow specification.

title: 2  Principles of trustworthy assistance
text:
2.8 Putting the principles together
The five principles form a connected system. Inspectable artifacts establish a shared basis for the work. Explicit state provides continuity. Events and rules make action predictable. Tools connect findings to evidence. Human judgment sets the boundary of authority and accountability.
If any one element is missing, the workflow becomes harder to evaluate and trust. Together, the principles provide the foundation for the example-first, AI-first SDLC defined in Chapter 4.

title: 3  Onboarding an AI agent
text:
3.1 The onboarding analogy
Imagine that a new team member has joined. They recently finished school and understand the basics of clinical trials. They know what a protocol and statistical analysis plan (SAP) are, but they do not yet know standard operating procedures (SOPs), computing environment, folder structure, naming conventions, or review habits of your organization.
For their first assignment, you choose a simple task:
The task is deliberately small. You are onboarding them more on the workflow than the tool. Can the new colleague find and use the relevant documents? Can they identify the correct analysis population, handle missing values, notice protocol deviations, and report findings and assumptions?
Now replace “new colleague” with “AI agent.” Almost everything you would set up for a person still applies, but each item has to become something written down rather than something learned by sitting nearby.
The model matters, but a more capable model does not define an acceptable result. The surrounding task and workflow establish the evidence, boundaries, and human decision rights.

title: 3  Onboarding an AI agent
text:
3.2 What an AI agent is
A large language model (LLM) interprets supplied context and generates a response. The context includes the request, instructions, documents, prior messages, and tool results made available for the current interaction.
An AI agent adds a controlled execution loop around the model:

interpret the task and select a next step;
use an allowed tool, such as a document reader or R;
observe the tool result and update the plan; and
continue until the task is complete, blocked, or requires approval.

The main components are distinguished by their responsibilities:







Component
Responsibility




LLM
Interpret context, plan steps, and draft an explanation


Harness
Assemble context, call the model, invoke tools, record events, and control the loop


Model gateway
Route model requests and apply authentication, logging, or policy controls


Tool interfaces
Perform observable actions such as reading a PDF, querying data, or running R


Working state
Hold messages, plans, tool results, and unresolved questions during the interaction


Accessible environment
Limit the files, commands, APIs, network destinations, and credentials the agent can reach









Figure 3.1: A general AI-agent architecture. The harness coordinates the model, working state, and tool interfaces. The accessible environment limits which resources the agent can reach.



Two distinctions are important:

Working state is not durable project memory. Rules and decisions that must survive an interaction belong in versioned artifacts rather than only in chat history.
Tool access is not authority. The technical ability to edit a file or call an API does not grant approval or decision rights.

Tools also do not make a model reliable by default. An agent can omit a source, resolve ambiguity silently, write code without executing it, misread a tool result, or follow an instruction from an untrusted artifact. Bounded access, observable tool use, and human review limit the consequences and make failures easier to detect.

title: 3  Onboarding an AI agent
text:
3.3 Make the task contract explicit
The task contract records the expectations for a delegated task. It is a small specification for the assignment rather than a prompt-writing trick.








Part
Question
Age-summary example




Objective
What should be produced?
An age summary and a short review note


Inputs
Which artifact versions govern the work?
A public protocol and a named synthetic CSV snapshot


Scope
Which population and variables are relevant?
The protocol-defined population and AGE


Output
What must the result contain?
Statistics, executed R code, sources, assumptions, and questions


Boundaries
Which data, tools, and destinations are allowed?
Read-only access to the two linked public artifacts


Escalation
When should the agent stop or ask?
Missing artifacts, ambiguous scope, conflicting evidence, or suspected data issues



A task contract does not require every uncertainty to be resolved in advance. It requires uncertainties to be visible so the agent does not silently turn an assumption into a decision.

3.4 A minimal AI-adoption example

title: 3  Onboarding an AI agent
section: 3.5 Why the demonstration is adoption, not a workflow
text:
3.5 Why the demonstration is adoption, not a workflow
The demonstration leaves the underlying process unchanged. A person manually starts the work, supplies the context, interprets the response, and decides what happens next.







Missing workflow capability
What the demonstration does instead




Defined trigger
A person chooses when to send the prompt


Controlled artifact retrieval
Links are assembled inside one interaction


Repeatable execution contract
The agent may choose a different path on another run


Predetermined benchmark
The returned result is inspected after it is produced


Durable state
Findings and decisions remain in the interaction unless recorded elsewhere


Explicit decision record
Human follow-up is expected but not captured by the task



The distinction is not a criticism of prompt-based use. AI adoption is a fast way to discover whether a task is valuable and what an agent can accomplish. The single result reveals the artifacts, tools, assumptions, exceptions, and human decisions that a future workflow must govern.

title: 3  Onboarding an AI agent
section: 3.6 From one result to an AI-first workflow
text:
3.6 From one result to an AI-first workflow
The next design step is not a longer prompt. It is to turn the useful parts of the interaction into a bounded, repeatable process: define an event, version the task contract, retrieve the governing artifacts, execute deterministic checks, measure the result against a benchmark, record the human decision, and use that state in the next run.
The applied examples in this book make that transition through the shared AI-first SDLC defined in Chapter 4. Each example begins with a bounded business problem and develops the artifacts, evidence, and decision points needed to move beyond a single prompt.

title: 4  The AI-first SDLC
text:
4.1 Why an AI-first workflow needs a lifecycle
Imagine that a statistical programmer asks an agent to review a table program. The agent finds a rounding problem and explains it clearly. The result is useful, but it leaves several questions unanswered.
These questions cannot be answered by improving the prompt alone. They concern the process used to develop and operate the workflow. That process is the AI-first software development lifecycle, abbreviated AI-first SDLC.
The word software includes more than application code. An AI-first workflow may contain R functions, agent instructions, business rules, retrieval logic, tool interfaces, test cases, evaluation data, release configuration, and monitoring rules. It also depends on human roles and decisions. The lifecycle develops this complete working system.
The six stages in this chapter are adapted from the conventional SDLC and from Anthropic’s AI-Native SDLC Playbook, which connects stages through committed artifacts and human gates. Anthropic’s security perspective on its lifecycle also emphasizes bounded access, deterministic and agentic review, monitoring, and human accountability. The sources use the term AI-native; this book uses AI-first SDLC to keep the focus on developing a bounded AI-first workflow.

title: 4  The AI-first SDLC
text:
Will the same check run after the next code change?
Which rules govern the review? What counts as a successful finding?
Who decides whether the code must change?
What happens when the agent misses a known problem?

title: 4  The AI-first SDLC
section: 4.2 Distinguish the development loop from the agent loop
text:
4.2 Distinguish the development loop from the agent loop
Chapter 3 describes the execution loop inside an agent interaction: the model selects a step, uses a tool, observes the result, and continues. The AI-first SDLC is a different loop. It governs how the workflow itself changes over days, releases, and repeated use.









Agent execution loop
AI-first SDLC




Unit of work
One assigned task
The workflow as a maintained system


Time scale
One interaction or run
Multiple development and operating cycles


State
Messages, plans, and tool results
Versioned requirements, code, evaluations, releases, and monitoring decisions


Success
Completion of the assigned task
Sustained performance against the workflow’s intended outcome


Human role
Review exceptions and make the task decision
Approve intent, design, benchmark, release, and improvement



An agent may assist in every SDLC stage, but it should not approve its own requirements, evaluation, release, or proposed policy change.

text:
4.3 Artifacts connect the six stages
The lifecycle uses six stages:

Plan — Frame the workflow
Design — Specify the workflow
Build — Prototype the workflow
Test — Benchmark and evaluate
Deploy — Operationalize the workflow
Maintain — Monitor and improve

Figure 4.1: The AI-first SDLC is a loop connected by six accepted artifacts.





Each stage ends with a canonical artifact:









Stage

A committed artifact is durable, versioned, reviewable, and accepted into the team’s system of record. It does not have to be a long document or a Git commit. Depending on the environment, it may be a Markdown file, YAML specification, R package, test report, approved ticket, release entry, or dashboard snapshot.
The artifact becomes the shared interface between Biometrics and engineering. It records the decision in terms both groups can inspect, and its acceptance provides the event that begins the next stage.

section: 4.10 How the applied examples use the lifecycle
text:
4.10 How the applied examples use the lifecycle
Each applied example begins with a clinical problem and then follows the same six stages. The canonical artifacts make examples comparable even when their technical implementations differ.
The artifact’s level of completion depends on the example’s declared maturity:







Maturity
Expected artifact evidence




Design pattern
Workflow brief and task contract are concrete; later artifacts describe the proposed implementation and known gaps


Reproducible prototype
Code, data, tests, expected results, and benchmark report can be rerun


Comparative survey
A shared task contract and benchmark compare time-stamped product behavior


Reference implementation
Release and monitoring evidence come from a maintained implementation



An example may revisit an earlier stage when evidence changes the design. A failed benchmark can return to Build, an inaccessible artifact can return to Design, and a monitoring signal can return to Plan. The headings provide a shared reasoning structure, not a claim that development proceeds in a straight line.

title: 4  The AI-first SDLC
text:
4.11 Summary
The AI-first SDLC organizes development around six questions and six committed artifacts: the Plan stage produces the workflow brief, Design the task contract, Build the prototype, Test the benchmark report, Deploy the release record, and Maintain the monitoring report.
The artifacts allow Biometrics workflow owners and AI engineers to define the same work, inspect the same evidence, and concentrate human judgment at explicit gates. Their sequence creates continuity; the monitoring report closes the loop by providing evidence for the next workflow brief.

title: 5  Rounding in analysis and reporting
text:
5.1 Define the rules before checking the work
Imagine a Biometrics team preparing an adverse-event table. The display specification requires integer percentages and includes only terms whose percentages meet a reporting threshold. Only after the table is produced does a reviewer notice that team convention turns 2.5 percent into 3, while R’s default round() function turns it into 2. This halfway case is called a decimal tie. The correction is small. The deeper problem is that the organization’s rounding rules were not explicit enough to check when the code changed.
Common programming languages differ in their default handling of decimal ties:
The lesson is not that one language is correct. A language default is an implementation choice, not organizational policy.
This chapter explores the problem, writes three related rules down, and sends one prompt to an agent to check a real R package against the first rule. The exercise can reveal a real finding, but a one-off prompt does not produce a workflow. In the AI-first SDLC from Chapter 4, the problem, rules, scope, and evidence gathered here are discovery inputs rather than completed Plan or Design artifacts. Chapter 6 starts from those inputs and the limits identified here.
A reviewer cannot ask an agent or a team member to verify conventions that exist only in habit. The first task is not writing a prompt. It is producing a short, versioned set of statements describing what the organization requires.
crumbs: 5  Rounding in analysis and reporting

title: 5  Rounding in analysis and reporting
text:
5.1.1 Three business rules
This example uses three separate, illustrative business rules: BR-001, BR-002, and BR-003. They are not approved industry standards, and they are not the stated rules of any package reviewed here.
The rules answer three different questions: how ties are rounded, when rounding occurs, and how display precision is preserved. The exercise below checks only tie behavior; rounding stage and display precision remain explicit gaps.

BR-001: Values intended as exact decimal ties are rounded half away from zero. A displayed value is never a negative zero.


BR-002: Calculations use unrounded values; rounding occurs once, when the final result is prepared for display.


BR-003: Display precision is specified for each reported statistic and preserved, including trailing zeros.

BR-003 covers a problem that is easy to overlook because it is not arithmetic. The values 76, 76.0, and 76.00 are numerically equal, but they communicate different precision in a table. A program can calculate the intended number and still produce an output that violates a reporting convention.






NoteBeyond this example: A community rounding skill



This book uses all three rules to define the policy, then deliberately limits the skill design in Chapter 6 to BR-001. A broader rounding skill covering tie method, rounding stage, and display precision is being developed through RConsortium/pharma-skills issue #208. As of 2026-09-06, the issue defines the first benchmark and states that the skill does not yet exist. Interested readers can follow the issue as the community turns the three-rule policy into a tested skill.




5.1.2 Define which calls are in scope
Naming BR-001 is not enough. The rule must also say where it applies. A request to check that source code “properly rounds half away from zero” does not say which calls are in scope, and the answer changes completely depending on that definition. BR-001 therefore carries this scope:

For this review, include any function call that can change a numeric value displayed in a report or used to decide which rows the report includes. Formatting functions round as a side effect of display, so formatC(), sprintf(), and format() are candidates. Finding one round() call does not establish complete coverage.

That clause is the difference between a review that inspects one function name and a review that inspects the calls that actually reach the table. The rest of this chapter shows how much difference it makes.

title: 5  Rounding in analysis and reporting
text:
5.2 An exploratory request
The review target is Merck/metalite.ae v0.1.4, an open source R package that analyzes adverse events from ADaM data and produces tables, listings, and figures using the metalite data structure. The release is pinned to commit bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b.
A reviewer beginning a check against BR-001 might write this:

In metalite.ae v0.1.4 (commit https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/tree/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b), verify whether the R source uses round half away from zero for analysis and reporting. If not, identify the source and draft a GitHub issue to report the finding.

The request names a target and a rule while leaving the search method open. That gives the agent room to inspect the package, follow unexpected paths, and surface assumptions, which is useful during an exploratory review. The same freedom makes the result difficult to evaluate or repeat: the request does not define the minimum files that must be covered, the evidence needed to demonstrate a violation, or who classifies the finding. A reusable workflow must clarify those evaluation and decision boundaries without prescribing every step in the agent’s reasoning.

5.2.1 Try it yourself
Send the following prompt to arena.ai before reading the rest of this chapter. The prompt deliberately leaves the investigation open. It fixes the target and rule, then lets the agent choose how to search, which clues to follow, and what supporting evidence to gather.
Review the R source of the metalite.ae package at release v0.1.4 and the exact
commit linked below.

Verify whether it follows BR-001: values intended as exact decimal ties must
round half away from zero, and a displayed value must never be a negative zero.

Release: v0.1.4
Pinned commit:
https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/tree/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b

If evidence diverges from the rule, draft a GitHub issue.






NoteExample output



Arena.ai cannot create a GitHub issue. A person manually copied one response to this prompt into issue #249; neither Arena.ai nor the skill designed in the next chapter posted it. Treat the saved response as an example to review, not as the answer key or a finding approved by the package maintainers.


Agent responses vary between runs, and that variability is part of the lesson. Do not treat any particular response as the answer key. Judge the response you receive by asking:

Did it inspect formatting functions as well as round()?
Did it follow wrappers or other unexpected paths through the code?
Did it give locations at the pinned commit rather than general advice?
Did it demonstrate behavior at ties of both signs?
Did it state what it checked and what it did not?
Did it distinguish observed behavior from the assumption that BR-001 applies?
Did it keep source evidence, causal explanations, defect classification, and proposed solutions separate?

The prompt did not ask the agent to search only for round(). It also did not prescribe a function catalog or a minimum search procedure. The response saved in issue #249 interpreted the request broadly: it examined an explicit round() call, formatting helpers, decimal-tie examples, negative-zero output, and a possible effect on report filtering. That breadth illustrates the value of leaving an exploratory investigation open.
crumbs: 5  Rounding in analysis and reporting

title: 5  Rounding in analysis and reporting
section: 5.3 What one exploratory prompt cannot provide
text:
5.3 What one exploratory prompt cannot provide
Reviewing the saved response makes that response easier to judge. It does not turn the interaction into a workflow. No workflow brief has been accepted, and no task contract specifies a repeatable check.
Leaving the search open can reveal functions, wrappers, and code paths that the reviewer did not anticipate. The tradeoff is that the prompt sets no minimum check against which another run can be compared. Four workflow capabilities are still missing:

Coverage assurance. A response can state which files and rules it checked, but the interaction provides no required file list or minimum set of checks against which to test that claim. Silence is not evidence that every file or rule was reviewed.
Repeatability. Repeatability does not require the agent to reason the same way on every run. It does require a stable minimum procedure and expected results. The exploratory prompt supplies none of those controls, so another run can follow a different path and return different coverage.
Separation of checks from judgment. The response can mix reproduced observations, causal explanations, provisional triage, and proposed decisions. A workflow must label deterministic evidence separately from agent judgment and human classification.
A named human gate. The prompt requests a draft but does not name who classifies each finding as a defect, a documented convention, an accepted exception, or not applicable, or who decides whether to post it.

These are workflow requirements, not criticisms of the response’s breadth. The gaps, together with the problem, rules, and reviewed evidence, are inputs to Plan in Chapter 6. The next chapter organizes them into a workflow brief, then carries them into a task contract in Design. That design establishes required checks as a minimum while preserving a separate exploratory pass.
crumbs: 5  Rounding in analysis and reporting

title: 5  Rounding in analysis and reporting
text:
5.4 Summary
Rounding looks like a settled question until two tools disagree at a tie. The disagreement is not a bug in a language; it is an unwritten policy. Writing the three rules down makes the policy explicit. Defining where BR-001 applies is what makes the response reviewable. The later source review contrasts one direct round() match with eight formatC() candidates.
An exploratory prompt can surface useful candidates and testable claims, and it may reveal paths the reviewer did not anticipate. Reading its output requires separating candidate evidence, reproduced observations, causal explanations, and proposed decisions. Turning that review into a workflow additionally requires assured coverage, repeatable minimum checks and a recorded human decision. Chapter 6 begins the lifecycle by turning those gaps into workflow requirements.
crumbs: 5  Rounding in analysis and reporting

title: 6  Building the rounding check as an agent skill
text:
6.1 Plan — Frame the workflow
During clinical development, the R scripts used for analysis and reporting may change over time. The developer must repeat the rounding review from Chapter 5. The saved response preserves candidate locations, example outputs, explanations, and a proposed solution, but not a repeatable method: which functions must be searched, which ties must be tested, how coverage is recorded, or when to stop before posting an issue. The draft survived the handoff. The ability to reproduce and evaluate it did not.
Chapter 5 established three business rules, defined the scope of BR-001, and showed how to read an exploratory response as a draft rather than an answer key. It also named four things a prompt cannot provide: coverage, repeatability, separation of fixed checks from judgment, and a named human gate. This chapter turns those gaps into requirements and specifies each stage of the AI-first SDLC from Chapter 4.
The AI-Native SDLC Playbook lesson on skills as institutional knowledge describes a skill as a way to make owned, written knowledge operational. This chapter adapts that idea to Biometrics: BR-001 is the source of truth, the rule owner controls it, and the skill tells an agent how to apply it during a bounded review. The skill remains an advisory control. Fixed scripts can produce repeatable evidence, but a person still approves the rule and classifies the finding.
The Build stage develops the same proposed skill in two examples. The first uses only SKILL.md, making the trigger, instruction, boundaries, and output visible in one place. The second keeps that entry point small and adds a rule reference, fixed scripts, and a report template. Comparing them shows when one file is enough and when additional resources are justified.
The chapter has one main finding: start with one inspectable instruction, then add a resource only when the task contract explains what behavior it should improve.
crumbs: 6  Building the rounding check as an agent skill

title: 6  Building the rounding check as an agent skill
text:
6.1.1 Turn the prompt’s limits into requirements
The four gaps in Chapter 5 are not additional metalite.ae defects. They are limitations of the one-off review, and each one becomes a workflow requirement:

replace reviewer memory with a written minimum procedure while leaving room for the agent to investigate beyond it;
report coverage for every run, including rules left unchecked;
keep fixed, repeatable checks separate from exploratory agent work and judgment in the output; and
name the human who classifies each finding, and stop before any external action.

A fifth design need appears when the review is repeated: a previously reviewed call should not require the same triage on every run. The rule owner may approve an allowlist entry with its reason and source version. The call remains visible in coverage, and a source change returns it to review.
The function catalog is a required starting point, not a ceiling. The agent can follow wrappers, helper functions, or other unexpected code paths, but it must label candidates found through that exploratory pass separately.


6.1.2 Canonical artifact: Workflow brief

Objective: Specify a check that finds calls able to round a displayed value or a value used in a report decision, tests them against the half-away-from-zero rule, and can be performed by a reviewer who did not design it.
Inputs: One R source folder at a pinned commit, BR-001 v1.0, the precision used by each relevant output, rule-owner-selected comparison behavior, and any approved allowlist.
Intended output: A versioned draft review report containing candidate locations, triage reasons, probe results, coverage, unchecked rules, and items requiring a human decision.
Baseline evidence: Issue #249 shows what an open investigation can contribute. The manually reviewed source inventory and tie probe below provide the answer key, not measured workflow performance.
Value hypothesis: A stable minimum check plus an exploratory pass will reduce repeated manual search. Moving the controlled rule, fixed checks, and report structure into separate resources should make evidence and coverage more reproducible than the one-file baseline.
Agent contribution: Run the fixed checks when an implementation exists, search beyond the catalog for unexpected paths, read surrounding code, explain evidence, and draft output. Label fixed and exploratory results separately.
Human decision: The rule owner approves the procedure and classifies each result as a defect, documented convention, accepted exception, or not applicable.
Success measures: Select the skill for applicable requests and not for unrelated requests; find every deliberately noncompliant test call; flag no compliant test example; attach rule-specific probe evidence to every finding; state what was not checked; and distinguish catalog results from exploratory findings. Under an identical environment, the resource-backed version must preserve its fixed scan output, probe output, and required report fields across repeated runs.
Main risks: A narrow search can produce a convincing false clean report, and a polished skill description can create confidence before the underlying checks have been implemented and benchmarked.

The Plan gate is the rule owner’s decision that a repeatable check is worth building. The accepted workflow brief initiates Design.
crumbs: 6  Building the rounding check as an agent skill

title: 6  Building the rounding check as an agent skill
text:
6.2 Design — Specify the workflow

6.2.1 Carry the rule and its scope clause forward unchanged
BR-001, BR-002, and BR-003, stated in Chapter 5, are separate business rules. BR-001 requires exact decimal ties to round half away from zero and prohibits a displayed negative zero. BR-002 requires calculations to use unrounded values and to round once for display. BR-003 requires display precision to be specified and preserved. Each rule is version 1.0 in this example.
The scope clause attached to BR-001 defines which calls are in scope: any call that can change a numeric value displayed in a report or used to decide which rows the report includes. It therefore places formatC(), sprintf(), and format() among the candidates.
This workflow checks only BR-001. BR-002 and BR-003 remain explicit gaps, declared in every run rather than left unmentioned. For this exercise, the illustrative rule owner selects the documented behavior of cards::round5() as the comparison behavior. A future implementation must pin the package version and test the selected behavior, including values near a tie. This is not an industry endorsement.


6.2.2 Design two increments of the same skill
The Agent Skills specification requires only a directory containing SKILL.md. Its header contains name and description, and the name must match the directory name. Directories such as references/, scripts/, and assets/ are optional. That makes it possible to start with one file and add structure only when the workflow needs it.
This chapter uses two build examples rather than treating the complete folder layout as the starting point:








Build example
Contents
Question it answers




1. One-file skill
SKILL.md only
Can one inspectable instruction make the rule, trigger, procedure, boundaries, and output visible?


2. Resource-backed skill
SKILL.md plus references/, scripts/, and assets/
Which limitations require controlled context, fixed execution, or a stable report form?



Both examples describe the same workflow and use the same skill name. The second is an evolution of the first, not a separate workflow or a second turn through the lifecycle. The task contract defines the behavior that both versions must attempt to provide and identifies where the one-file version is not strong enough.


6.2.3 Canonical artifact: Task contract

Objective: Report candidate divergences from BR-001 in one named R source folder.
Trigger: An approved on-demand request; automated triggers remain future options.
Required context: Target commit, source folder, BR-001 v1.0, the function catalog, the selected comparison function and its version, required display precision, and any approved allowlist.
Fixed, repeatable checks (deterministic work): Scan a catalog of possible rounding and numeric-to-text functions, then probe each provisionally in-scope numeric call with decimal ties of both signs at its required precision and with negative values that should display as zero.
Agent work: Search beyond the catalog for wrappers and other unexpected paths, provisionally determine whether each candidate affects a displayed numeric value or a report decision, explain any divergence, and draft the report.
Required output: file:line, source expression, probe result, supported explanation or unresolved cause, discovery method, triage reason, coverage, execution environment, and unchecked rules. Results from the catalog scan and exploratory search remain labeled separately.
Boundaries: Read and test only; no source edits, policy changes, classification approval, or external posting.
Stop conditions: Missing rule version, unreadable files, unresolved display precision or tie intent, a documented conflicting convention, or failed checks.
Human decision: The rule owner confirms triage, classifies each finding, approves exceptions, and authorizes any communication.

The contract describes the target behavior. The one-file example can require the scan and probe, but it cannot make their execution deterministic by itself. The resource-backed example assigns that fixed work to separately testable scripts while leaving exploration and triage with the agent.
The Design gate is approval of the rule scope, task contract, two-increment build plan, and stop conditions by the rule owner and an R programmer. Acceptance authorizes a prototype, not a finding or a code change, and initiates Build.
crumbs: 6  Building the rounding check as an agent skill

title: 6  Building the rounding check as an agent skill
text:
6.3 Build — Prototype the workflow
The Build stage makes the proposed skill visible in two increments. These are manuscript listings, not files distributed by the book. They show how a team could start with one inspectable instruction and then add resources in response to evidence about its limitations.

6.3.1 Example 1: Start with SKILL.md only
The smallest conforming skill is one directory containing one SKILL.md:
rounding-rule-review/
  SKILL.md
The following proposed file makes the trigger, rule, procedure, output, and stop conditions visible together:
---
name: rounding-rule-review
description: Reviews a bounded R source tree for BR-001. Use when a
  reviewer needs call locations, tie probes, coverage, and draft
  findings for human review.
---

# Rounding rule review

## Required inputs

- A pinned source commit and one R source folder
- BR-001 v1.0 and the required precision for each relevant output
- The selected comparison behavior and its version
- Any rule-owner-approved allowlist

## Rule and scope

Apply BR-001: values intended as exact decimal ties round half away from zero,
and a displayed value is never a negative zero.

Include any call that can change a numeric value displayed in a report or used
to decide which rows the report includes. Formatting calls are candidates.

## Procedure

1. List every `.R` file in scope.
2. Search for `round()`, `signif()`, `formatC()`, `sprintf()`, `format()`,
   `prettyNum()`, and `as.character()`.
3. Search beyond that catalog for wrappers and unexpected rounding paths.
4. Read each candidate in context and record whether it can affect a displayed
   numeric value or a report decision.
5. Probe each provisionally in-scope call at its required precision with
   positive and negative decimal ties. For display calls, also test negative
   values that should display as zero.
6. Keep catalog results, exploratory candidates, probe output, provisional
   triage, and human classification separate.

## Required report

Record `file:line`, source expression, discovery method, triage reason, probe
result, supported explanation or unresolved cause, files examined, exclusions,
execution environment, unchecked rules, and items requiring human review.

## Stop and escalate

Stop when the rule version, required precision, tie intent, source, or
comparison behavior is unresolved, or when a check fails. Do not edit source,
change policy, approve a classification, or post an external issue.
This one-file version is useful. A reviewer can inspect the whole instruction, the agent can discover it from its description, and a rule owner can review a single change. It is also only an advisory procedure. The agent still chooses how to perform the catalog search and tie probes, the rule is coupled to the operating instructions, and prose alone does not ensure that every run produces the same coverage record or output structure.
Those limits are evidence for the next build increment. They are not reasons to skip the one-file version: a small, low-risk task may not justify more machinery.


6.3.2 Example 2: Add resources to improve behavior
For this review, the task contract requires stronger separation of policy, fixed evidence, and presentation. The second example keeps SKILL.md as the entry point and adds only the resources needed for those requirements:
rounding-rule-review/
  SKILL.md
  references/
    br-001.md
  scripts/
    scan-rounding-calls.R
    probe-tie-behavior.R
  assets/
    review-report-template.md
The revised SKILL.md becomes shorter because it orchestrates the resources instead of carrying all their detail:
---
name: rounding-rule-review
description: Reviews a bounded R source tree for BR-001. Use when a
  reviewer needs call locations, tie probes, coverage, and draft
  findings for human review.
---

# Rounding rule review

1. Read [`references/br-001.md`](references/br-001.md). Confirm its version,
   scope, rule owner, selected comparison behavior, and approved allowlist.
2. Run `scripts/scan-rounding-calls.R` on the approved R source folder. Preserve
   the complete file inventory and catalog candidates.
3. Search beyond the catalog for wrappers and unexpected paths. Label these
   candidates as exploratory.
4. Read every candidate in context. Record provisional triage without silently
   removing excluded candidates from coverage.
5. For each provisionally in-scope call, run
   `scripts/probe-tie-behavior.R` at the required precision.
6. Complete the
   [`assets/review-report-template.md`](assets/review-report-template.md).
   Keep fixed output, exploratory work, agent judgment, and human classification
   separate.
7. Stop before source changes, policy changes, classification approval, or any
   external posting.

If required context is missing or a script fails, record the problem and stop.
Each added resource has one job and one intended effect:









Component
Contents
Behavior it is intended to improve
What it cannot decide




SKILL.md
Trigger, sequence, boundaries, and escalation
Consistent activation and orchestration
Whether a candidate is a confirmed defect


references/br-001.md
Rule text, scope, version, owner, comparison behavior, and allowlist
Traceability to controlled institutional knowledge
Whether the policy should change


scripts/scan-rounding-calls.R
File inventory and required function catalog
Repeatable minimum coverage
Every dynamically constructed or uncataloged path


scripts/probe-tie-behavior.R
Fixed inputs, comparison results, and environment capture
Reproducible numeric evidence
Whether a source value was intended as an exact decimal tie


assets/review-report-template.md
Required fields and separate evidence sections
More consistent, reviewable output
Whether an explanation or classification is correct



This layout uses progressive disclosure. The agent sees the name and description when selecting a skill, loads the SKILL.md instructions when the skill applies, and reads or runs the other resources only when directed. Moving details out of SKILL.md therefore improves separation without hiding the path the agent must follow.


6.3.3 How the resource-backed version performs the check
The proposed scanner covers direct calculation functions such as round() and signif(), formatting functions such as formatC(), sprintf(), format(), and prettyNum(), and conversions such as as.character(). It produces candidates, not findings. The agent then explores beyond the catalog, reads each candidate in context, and provisionally determines whether it can affect a displayed numeric value or a report decision.
The probe runs only for provisionally in-scope numeric calls. It tests positive and negative decimal ties at the precision required by each call and, for display calls, negative values that should display as zero. It places the observed result beside the selected result and reports PASS or FAIL. If the required precision or intended tie cannot be determined, the workflow records the unresolved context and stops.






NoteOptional technical detail: Comparison call



The proposed probe obtains the selected comparison result with this call. Readers do not need to follow its syntax to understand the comparison.
approved <- cards::round5(x, digits = required_digits)
This call is a benchmark comparison for the exercise, not a proposed fix for metalite.ae. A future implementation must record the cards version, test values near a tie, and document how it decides that an input is intended as an exact decimal tie.




6.3.4 Preserve the decisions that made the check useful
The written procedure must preserve three decisions:

Use the function catalog as a minimum check, then search beyond it for wrappers and unexpected code paths. Record whether each candidate came from the catalog or the exploratory pass, and classify whether it affects display or a report decision.
Probe both direct rounding and formatting behavior at the precision used by each provisionally in-scope call, including negative values that should display as zero. Record the R version, and explain tie mode and binary representation as distinct causes.
Write findings to a draft and stop before any source change or posting a GitHub issue.

It must also state these limits:

A scanner can miss calls that are constructed only while the program runs.
An exploratory pass can find patterns outside the catalog, but it cannot prove complete coverage.
If the number of decimal places cannot be determined, the review stops.
An approved helper remains a candidate until the rule owner approves an allowlist entry with a reason and source version.
Only BR-001 is checked; BR-002 and BR-003 remain gaps.







WarningWhen not to use this skill



Do not use this design for nonnumeric reports or for reviews of rounding stage and display precision, which require BR-002 and BR-003. For a genuinely one-off review, the rule owner may decide that the exploratory prompt in Chapter 5 is proportionate.








NoteGo further: Review all three rounding rules



The two build examples in this chapter remain intentionally bounded to BR-001. The proposed benchmark in RConsortium/pharma-skills issue #208 extends the review to all three rules. It asks a future skill to trace relevant operations from R package report entry points, execute reproducible witnesses, and report separate verdicts for tie method, rounding stage, and display precision.
The broader Pharma Skills repository is an open, community-contributed catalog for pharmaceutical R&D. Readers can inspect its skill packages, benchmark proposals, and Agent Skill Development Lifecycle to see how agent skills can support AI-first work on open source R packages. The repository’s skills remain drafting aids that require independent review under the user’s own quality process.




6.3.5 Try the intended behavior without installing the skill
The book does not provide either skill version to Arena.ai. This exercise sends the intended behavior as a prompt so that a reader can inspect a fresh response. It demonstrates why the definition of which calls are in scope belongs in the skill rather than in a reviewer’s memory. Send this prompt to arena.ai:
Review the R source from metalite.ae v0.1.4 at the exact commit below for
BR-001: values intended as exact decimal ties must round half away from zero.
A displayed value must never be a negative zero.

Inspect every file under R/. First, run a required catalog scan for calls to
round(), signif(), sprintf(), formatC(), format(), prettyNum(), and
as.character(). Report every catalog match, including matches later excluded
from scope, and label these required-scan results separately from exploratory
candidates.

Include any function call that can change a numeric value displayed in a report
or used to decide which rows the report includes. Formatting functions can
round as a side effect of display. After the catalog scan, choose how to
investigate beyond those named functions, including wrappers or other
unexpected paths, and label those exploratory candidates.

Test decimal ties of both signs at the precision used by each in-scope call. For
display calls, also test negative values that should display as zero. For each
call, report its file and line, observed results, discovery method, R version,
coverage, and unchecked rules. Explain tie mode and binary representation
separately.

Draft a GitHub issue if evidence diverges from the rule, but do not post it. Do
not modify the repository or propose a code change.

Release: v0.1.4
Pinned commit:
https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/tree/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b
Arena.ai cannot create the GitHub issue. This is a behavioral preview, not a run of either proposed skill. Responses vary between runs, so compare the response with the pinned evidence below rather than expecting a particular answer.


6.3.6 Canonical artifact: Prototype
No executable prototype artifact exists. At design-pattern maturity, the two listings specify a one-file baseline and a resource-backed candidate. The second adds a controlled rule reference, fixed scan and probe interfaces, and a review-report template; it does not establish that behavior improved.
The Build gate remains open until an R programmer and the rule owner review a working version of both examples and confirm that the resource-backed candidate exposes fixed results separately from agent judgment. Only their acceptance would initiate a comparative benchmark against synthetic cases and the pinned source.
crumbs: 6  Building the rounding check as an agent skill

title: 6  Building the rounding check as an agent skill
text:
6.4 Test — Benchmark and evaluate
The benchmark must evaluate two different failure modes. First, does the agent select the skill for an applicable request and leave it unused for an unrelated request? Second, after selection, does the skill produce the required evidence and coverage? Adding files counts as improvement only if the second example performs better against predefined criteria.

6.4.1 Test whether the skill is selected
Both examples use the same name and description, so they should have the same selection behavior. A future implementation would present differently worded requests without naming the skill and record whether it loads:







Request
Expected selection behavior




Review a pinned R source folder for BR-001
Select the skill


Find rounding and numeric-formatting calls that can affect an R report
Select the skill and confirm that BR-001 is the governing rule


Explain why R and SAS differ at 2.5
Do not select the repository-review skill


Review when rounding occurs under BR-002
Do not select this BR-001 skill; use a workflow that explicitly covers BR-002


Review text padding in a nonnumeric report
Do not select the skill



Selection is necessary but not sufficient. A skill can load reliably and still miss files, probe the wrong precision, or mix evidence with judgment. Those behaviors require task-level cases.


6.4.2 Compare behavior with small test examples
A future benchmark would run the one-file baseline and the resource-backed candidate against the same five small synthetic R programs, with expected results recorded before either version runs. The cases include a compliant program, one formatC() display call that violates the tie and negative-zero clauses, one round() call before a threshold comparison, one approved-helper use, and one violation hidden behind a wrapper that is not named in the catalog. Together they test correct findings, false findings, allowlist handling, and the exploratory pass.
The book does not distribute these programs, so their outcomes are acceptance criteria rather than measured skill performance. They also show the cost of a broad search: it reduces the risk of a false clean report, but the workflow must retain and explain candidates that do not become findings.
The comparison records detection, false findings, missed problems, file and candidate coverage, required-field completion, repeated-run agreement, review time, and stopped runs. The resource-backed version is better only if it preserves the required findings while making the catalog scan, probe output, coverage record, and report structure more reproducible. Exploratory paths may still vary between runs and remain labeled separately.


6.4.3 Pinned source evidence for the answer key
All metalite.ae locations and results below refer to v0.1.4, released 2026-09-01 and pinned to commit bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b. The file count, candidate count, quoted locations, and probe results were manually reverified at this commit. They define reference evidence for a future benchmark; they are not output from the proposed skill. Every count, location, and result must be reverified again before use with another version or commit.
The evidence narrows in three steps:

A search for round( found one match, where a rounded percentage controls whether an adverse-event row passes a reporting threshold.
A catalog scan for seven function names found 21 candidate calls: one round(), eight formatC(), one sprintf(), and 11 as.character() calls.
Context review excluded 13 calls that operate on character or structural values, leaving eight in-scope calls: one report-filtering decision and seven calls that format values for display.







NoteWhy issue #249 is not the answer key



Issue #249 is a useful exploratory report, but its location list still requires context review. It includes R/fmt.R:37, where formatC() receives character text assembled after the numeric formatting at line 33. For character input, the formatC() documentation describes padding rather than numeric rounding. The issue also cites R/format_ae_exp_adj.R:203, which is not a formatting call; the direct formatC() call is at R/format_ae_exp_adj.R:208.
This difference illustrates why an agent’s candidate locations must be checked before they are counted as findings. The issue title, causal explanation, and proposed solution also remain proposals for human review. They are not evidence that BR-001 governs metalite.ae or that the proposed code would pass the benchmark below.


Those manually verified counts define the expected coverage of the required catalog scan. They do not prove that no relevant wrapper or unexpected code path exists. A future implementation must report the exploratory pass separately and test that pass with a seeded example that is not named in the catalog.
The in-scope calls show where the illustrative rule could affect an adverse-event report:



In-scope call
Role in the adverse-event report




R/format_ae_specific.R:330
Round a percentage before applying the row-inclusion threshold


R/fmt.R:33
Format percentages and total exposure


R/fmt.R:75
Format an estimate or mean


R/fmt.R:79
Format a standard deviation or standard error


R/fmt.R:99
Format a confidence-interval lower limit


R/fmt.R:100
Format a confidence-interval upper limit


R/fmt.R:122
Format a p-value above the display cutoff


R/format_ae_exp_adj.R:208
Format an exposure-adjusted event rate



The excluded formatC() call receives text that is already formatted rather than a numeric value (R/fmt.R:37). The sprintf() call builds JavaScript, and the 11 as.character() calls do not apply a specified decimal precision. They remain recorded as reviewed candidates rather than silently disappearing from the coverage statement.
The source accepts different precision arguments, so a complete implementation would construct decimal ties at the precision used by each call. The compact probe below uses one decimal place to compare the two underlying expressions. It was run with R 4.6.1 on arm64 macOS. formatC and round are observed results; approved is what BR-001 requires:
expressions:
  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
  round(x, digits = 1)

 input  formatC  round  approved
-76.05    -76.0  -76.0     -76.1
 -3.05     -3.0   -3.0      -3.1
 -2.05     -2.0   -2.0      -2.1
 -1.05     -1.1   -1.0      -1.1
 -0.05     -0.1   -0.0      -0.1
  0.05      0.1    0.0       0.1
  1.05      1.1    1.0       1.1
  2.05      2.0    2.0       2.1
  3.05      3.0    3.0       3.1
 76.05     76.0   76.0      76.1

formatC disagreements: 6 of 10
round disagreements: 10 of 10


6.4.4 Keep the two causes distinct
The probe uses one-decimal ties rather than the simpler zero-decimal ties of Chapter 5 for a reason: at one decimal place, two separate causes are visible, and only one of them can be predicted from reading the source. The divergence is not explained by one blanket claim about “banker’s rounding.” One cause determines the direction at a true tie; the other places the stored number slightly above or below the intended tie:

Tie mode. The Base R documentation describes round() as using round-to-nearest-even at a true tie. When a tie is exactly representable in binary, such as 2.5 at zero decimals, both tested expressions return 2 rather than the rule’s 3.
Binary representation. Most one-decimal ties are not stored exactly. For example, 2.05 is stored just below the intended tie, so formatting the stored value produces 2.0. Other inputs can fall on the other side of the intended tie.

These causes interact, so source inspection alone cannot predict every direction. That is why the probe, not the reviewer’s reasoning, is the evidence. The probe also exposes the negative-zero risk: formatting the one-decimal result of round(-0.05, 1) produces -0.0. At zero decimals, formatC(-0.5, digits = 0, format = "f") produces -0. Both violate the negative-zero clause.


6.4.5 What both proposed implementations must reproduce
No skill has been run. The results above are the answer key for a future test. The benchmark applies the accuracy and boundary criteria below to both build examples. The resource-backed candidate is eligible for release only if it also preserves fixed outputs and required report fields across repeated runs.







Acceptance criterion

Do not apply the BR-001 procedure to 3 of 3 requests

6.4.6 Canonical artifact: Benchmark report
No benchmark report exists because no prototype has been implemented or run. At design-pattern maturity, this artifact is specified rather than populated. The manually verified source inventory and tie probe above form the reference answer key; they are not workflow performance results.
A future benchmark report must:

identify both skill versions, the target, workflow components, R environment, rule, comparison function, and their versions;
report skill-selection results for the five activation requests;
report results for all five synthetic cases and the pinned-source criteria;
record detected and missed problems, incorrect findings, stopped runs, coverage, reproducibility, review time, and triage agreement;
preserve fixed check output separately from agent exploration and judgment;
compare each version with the independently maintained answer key and with the other version; and
record limitations and the reviewers’ disposition.

The Test gate remains open. It requires the rule owner and an independent reviewer to accept an executed benchmark report; the person who wrote the procedure should not be the only person judging whether it works. Only that accepted report would initiate Deploy.

title: 6  Building the rounding check as an agent skill
text:
6.5 Deploy — Operationalize the workflow






ImportantDesign, not implementation



The triggers below are options for the owning team. No skill, CI workflow, or scheduled job has been committed or run.


The Deploy design connects a future accepted prototype to an advisory review process. It prepares a review record and stops before any external action unless a named human authorizes it. Issue #249 was posted manually from one response to the exploratory prompt in Chapter 5. That action occurred outside the workflow designed here. The public issue is not evidence that the skill was released, that BR-001 is a metalite.ae rule, or that the package maintainers confirmed the finding.
The team has three trigger options:

On demand: A reviewer requests the check. Setup is minimal, but the process still depends on someone remembering to ask.
On a proposed source-code change: The check runs when relevant reporting source changes. This is timely but requires rules that limit when it runs and control unnecessary findings.
Scheduled: The check runs before a release or after source changes. It can detect drift from approved behavior, but the finding may be separated from the change that caused it.

The one-file version is the teaching baseline, not the proposed release candidate. If the comparative benchmark is accepted, the resource-backed version is the candidate because its rule, fixed evidence, and report structure can be reviewed and versioned separately. A team could first place it in the repository-level skill location supported by its agent platform. Organization-wide distribution would require a separately approved owner, support model, and change process. This chapter specifies neither installation path.
The proposed first release is on demand and advisory. Pull-request or scheduled execution requires separate approval after benchmark evidence shows acceptable coverage and review burden. A schedule should not rerun unchanged source. The continuous, change-triggered check is a possible later destination, not the first release.

6.5.1 Canonical artifact: Release record

Status: Not released; this is the record structure required before use.
Candidate: The resource-backed version; the one-file version remains the benchmark baseline.
Release model: Manual and advisory; a reviewer requests one run.
Proposed versions: rounding-rule-review v1.0 and BR-001 v1.0.
Scope: One identified R source folder and commit per run.
Permissions: Read source, run approved local scripts, and write a draft report; no network writes.
Output: Versioned draft review report containing findings, probes, coverage, execution environment, limitations, run log, and an optional draft issue body.
Accountable human: The named rule owner approves release, classifications, exceptions, and any external communication.
Reversal: If released, disable the approved trigger and retain the run record. A normal advisory run changes no source or external system.

Because it was copied from an exploratory response outside this workflow, issue #249 is not the Deploy artifact or evidence that the Deploy gate passed. That gate is explicit rule-owner approval of the release record and any external communication. An accepted benchmark plus that approval would activate the chosen trigger and initiate Maintain. Neither event has occurred in this book.

title: 6  Building the rounding check as an agent skill
text:
6.6 Maintain — Monitor and improve

6.6.1 Make improvement a governed change
An operating check could suggest catalog additions, allowlist entries, triage patterns, or rule clarifications. Those are proposals. Before a change becomes active, the rule owner approves changes to references/br-001.md, an R programmer reviews script changes, and an independent reviewer adds or updates a test example. The workflow owner reviews changes to the trigger, instructions, and report template. The agent does not edit the rule against which it is evaluated.
The first list of improvements follows directly from known limitations:

Add a rule-owner-approved allowlist for compliant wrappers.
Record target commit, versions, files scanned, exclusions, probe output, triage reasons, and classifications in a run log.
Report files or expressions the check could not evaluate.
Keep this BR-001 skill bounded. Develop the comprehensive three-rule scope explicitly through the benchmark and review process tracked in RConsortium/pharma-skills issue #208 rather than silently expanding the active rule.



6.6.2 Canonical artifact: Monitoring report
There is no operating history because the book distributes no workflow. The monitoring report is therefore specified, not populated. A future report must show applicable requests that did and did not select the skill, unrelated requests that selected it incorrectly, runs by trigger, coverage, confirmed findings, false positives, missed defects, stopped runs, triage effort, and unresolved precision. It also records how long an approved BR-001 change takes to reach the skill and its tests, whether the active skill still names the current rule version, incidents, and approved changes.
The rule owner reviews that report and chooses among continued use, correction, retirement, or a new planning cycle. An accepted policy change, incident, or measured coverage gap is the event that starts the next cycle.

title: 6  Building the rounding check as an agent skill
text:
6.7 Summary
Chapter 5 showed that a written rule and one open prompt can produce useful candidates, examples, explanations, and a proposed solution. It did not treat that response as an answer key. The separate source review in this chapter identifies one round() call used in a report-filtering decision and seven in-scope numeric formatC() calls. Its one-decimal probe diverges from BR-001 in 10 of 10 round() results and 6 of 10 formatC() results in the recorded environment. These are differences from the illustrative rule, not a maintainer-approved defect classification. Tie mode and binary representation remain separate causes.
The first build example packages the trigger, BR-001, procedure, boundaries, and output in one SKILL.md. That is the minimal visible skill and may be proportionate for a small, low-risk review. The second example adds a controlled rule reference, fixed scan and probe interfaces, and a report template. Each resource addresses a named limitation while the agent continues to explore and perform provisional triage.
The design does not assume that more files produce better behavior. A future benchmark must compare both versions for skill selection, findings, false findings, coverage, output completeness, and reproducibility. The resource-backed version becomes a release candidate only if that evidence is accepted. An executable prototype, an accepted benchmark report, a release, and operating evidence remain future work.
Readers who want to continue beyond this bounded design can follow RConsortium/pharma-skills issue #208. It is the community workspace for extending the exercise into a comprehensive rounding skill and benchmark that cover BR-001, BR-002, and BR-003.
